title: Space budgets and problems at home

turns.speaker: Ash
turns.text: Somebody at the meeting said the moon budget would fix the housing waiting list, and the room just nodded.

turns.speaker: Vic
turns.text: It wouldn't, though. It's a rounding error against housing. That comparison always flatters the wrong side.

turns.speaker: Leila
turns.text: How much are we actually talking about?

turns.speaker: Vic
turns.text: Space is well under one per cent of the budget. Health is around a fifth. You could delete space entirely and nobody would notice it in a hospital.

turns.speaker: Ash
turns.text: That's a fair correction, but it's also an argument that would protect any small programme from any scrutiny.

turns.speaker: Vic
turns.text: True. So judge it on its own merits rather than against housing.

turns.speaker: Leila
turns.text: On its merits, the weather satellites alone probably justify the whole thing. Hurricane warnings went from hours to days.

turns.speaker: Ash
turns.text: That's satellites, though. Not people on the moon.

turns.speaker: Ash
turns.text: The robotic case is easy. The crewed case is the one that costs ten times as much and returns less science.

turns.speaker: Leila
turns.text: Which even a lot of space scientists say quietly.

turns.speaker: Vic
turns.text: The honest defence of crewed flight isn't scientific. It's that it's the only thing that makes anyone care, and the funding for the robots rides along behind it.

turns.speaker: Ash
turns.text: That's more persuasive than the science argument, actually.

turns.speaker: Leila
turns.text: It's also unmeasurable, which is why nobody puts it in the business case.

points: A claim that space spending could fix the housing waiting list is challenged as a misleading comparison.
Vic notes space is well under one per cent of the budget against roughly a fifth for health.
Ash accepts the correction but warns it would shield any small programme from scrutiny.
Leila argues weather satellites alone justify the spending, since hurricane warnings improved from hours to days.
Ash distinguishes robotic missions, which are easy to justify, from crewed flight, which costs far more and returns less science.
Vic's defence of crewed missions is that they sustain public interest and carry robotic funding with them, which Ash finds more persuasive though unmeasurable.
